articles.text:
The Bad Lands Cow Boy. Volume 1, Number 30. LITTLE MISSOURI, MEDORA P. O., DAK., AUGUST 28, 1884. Price $2.00 per Year.

BAD LANDS COW BOY, BY A. T. PACKARD. The Cow Boy is not published for fun, but for $2 per year. Advertising Rates made known on application. Standing Advertisements payable quarterly. Transient Advertisements and all Job work, money in sight. Address all communications to THE BAD LANDS COW BOY, MEDORA, DAKOTA. Entered at the post-office at Medora, Dak., as second class mail matter.

articles.text: The indorsement of Mr. L. N. Cary's candidacy by the Dickinson Press adds another important straw to show which way the wind blows. Mr. Cary, with the united support of Stark and Billings county is more than ever entitled to proper recognition at home, and the Cow Boy trusts that Morton county will heartily endorse the selection of her neighbors when the time comes. There should be unanimity of action in this matter west of the Missouri, and if there are others who had hoped to capture the legislative honors of 1884, let them gracefully bow to the combination which decrees otherwise.
articles.summary: The Cow Boy welcomes the Dickinson Press's endorsement of L. N. Cary for the legislature and urges Morton county to back him.

articles.headline: Railroad News.
articles.text: The steam shovel has been set to work east of town, supplying three gravel trains which are kept running between there and the washout. Owing to the seemingly great and continuous efforts it is expected that the repairs will be nearly completed this week.
articles.summary: A steam shovel east of town supplies gravel trains for repairing the washout, expected to be nearly fixed this week.

articles.text: J. T. Odell, vice-president, and C. C. Renshall, chief engineer, who have been here looking after the welfare of their road, left Tuesday on No. 2 on their special coach.
articles.summary: Northern Pacific vice-president J. T. Odell and chief engineer C. C. Renshall left Tuesday in their special coach.

articles.text: T. Greene, superintendent of the Missouri division, is registered at the Hotel de Mores. He is superintending the repairs and looking to the interests of his division.
articles.summary: Missouri division superintendent T. Greene is staying at the Hotel de Mores while overseeing repairs.

articles.text: Mr. C. C. Renshall, chief engineer of the Northern Pacific, through Mr. Grantier, foreman carpenter, is constructing a very substantial platform 35x60 across the west end of the new warehouse and placing a derrick to facilitate the handling of machinery and other heavy freight destined to the Black Hills; and when lumber arrives will petition off a neat office to be occupied by the forwarders. Meanwhile the painters are decorating the outside. When all this is completed we can boast of the neatest and most commodious freight warehouse in Dakota.
articles.summary: A 35x60 platform and derrick are being built at the new N. P. freight warehouse for Black Hills freight, with an office planned for the forwarders.

articles.headline: The Stage Line.
articles.text:
The Spearfish Register has the following in regard to the stage line:

The opening of this line we regard as fraught with speedy and early advantages and benefits to the Hills, of large magnitude and incalculable importance. It will at once bring to the attention of the country one of the richest and most valuable sections of the public domain in the great northwest, that has been unknown and is unsettled, that offers to the agriculturist and stockman attractions and inducement for settlement and cultivation that are unsurpassed in the west. The tide has already started in that direction, and the result is assuring and promising. At Valley creek, some 50 miles north of Minnesela, during the past two or three months, some twenty families have settled; while on the Little Missouri, about eight miles further north, about as many more have made a settlement, and they are all contented and satisfied with the land and the surroundings. Others have been in to see the country, and they return to induce others to locate on the land. The same is the case from Medora; and next year, both from the Northern Pacific on the north and the Hills on the south, a steady flow of immigrants will enter upon this domain, so that, by the middle of next summer it is fair to estimate 500 families will have found homes on the line of this stage route.
articles.summary: Reprint from the Spearfish Register praising the Medora–Black Hills stage line and reporting new settlements at Valley creek and on the Little Missouri.

articles.headline: Belfield Newslets.
articles.text: Bob Montgomery returned from the east on Monday, and his best friends failed to know him again. He came disguised as a Wall street broker.
articles.summary: Bob Montgomery returned to Belfield from the east on Monday.

articles.text: Mrs. F. H. Ertel and children bid adieu to Belfield on Sunday last, and will remain at St. Louis for the present.
articles.summary: Mrs. F. H. Ertel and children left Belfield for St. Louis on Sunday.

articles.text: Farmers Burke and Davis, from Dickinson, Sundayed here.
articles.summary: Farmers Burke and Davis of Dickinson spent Sunday at Belfield.

articles.text: There is some just indignation here against Supt. Greene of the Northern Pacific railrood. A few months ago he ordered the agent at this point to engage ponies and men to pursue some stolen cattle, promising fair pay. The cattle were found, and upon their return the men were asked to sign receipts for their claims, but as yet have failed to receive a penny. Some of the men believe they are being humbugged, and the temperature of their blood goes up as the thermometer goes down.
articles.summary: Belfield men hired by order of N. P. Supt. Greene to recover stolen cattle months ago say they have never been paid.

articles.text: Some Black Hills freight is moving, though the town, outside of the hotel, is not being benefitted by it.
articles.summary: Some Black Hills freight is moving through Belfield.

articles.text: Max Bass, who enjoys the monopoly of the hotel trade, is quietly getting rich and investing some of his spare cash in paints and oils, which gives his hostelry a highly distinguished appearance.
articles.summary: Max Bass is having his Belfield hotel painted.

articles.text: The new store of Martindale & Hanauer is doing a land office business, and the proprietors are pre-eminently popular.
articles.summary: The new Martindale & Hanauer store at Belfield is doing a brisk business.

articles.text: Mr. Pettit's family has arrived from Crook City in one of Pettit's finest stages, which is the most metropolitan thing that ever honored the town of Belfield.
articles.summary: Mr. Pettit's family arrived at Belfield from Crook City in one of his stages.

articles.headline: Arrested Horse Thieves.
articles.text: Scotty, or Henry Scott, was arrested at supper at Dixon's ranch last night by Deputy Sheriff Louis King. He was connected with Clay Layton, whose arrest was published in the Journal yesterday, in the theft of four horses from Archie Morton, of South Heart, Dak. The pair sold two of them here, another to Mr. Dixon and the fourth was traded for a rifle. They are hard characters and their arrest was well managed by the sheriff and his deputies.—[Yellowstone Journal.
articles.summary: Clipped from the Yellowstone Journal: Henry Scott, partner of Clay Layton in stealing four horses from Archie Morton of South Heart, was arrested at Dixon's ranch.

articles.headline: STOCK NOTES. $250 REWARD.
articles.text:
The above reward will be paid for information leading to the arrest of any person or persons setting fire to the grass in the cattle sections of Western Dakota.

N. P. Ref. Car Co.
Continental Cattle Co.
Hughes & Simpson.
Dorr Clark.
Clark & Plum.
Dickey Bros.
E. G. Paddock.
articles.summary: Seven cattle outfits offer $250 for the arrest of anyone setting grass fires in the cattle country of Western Dakota.

articles.headline: $50 Reward.
articles.text:
The above reward will be paid for the return of the following stock [or a?] proportionate reward will be paid for the return of any of them. The stock consists of the following horses:

One bay mare, one brown mare and one roan mare, all young and branded double or reverse P on left shoulder as advertised in our brand columns. Also one light sorrel pony, white legs and face and branded NC on left shoulder and triangle JP on right shoulder also as advertised in our brand columns.

GREGOR LANG, Medora, Dak.
articles.summary: Gregor Lang offers $50 for the return of three mares and a sorrel pony.

articles.headline: $125 Reward.
articles.text:
The above reward will be paid for the return of the team of large gray horses, half Norman breed, weighing twelve and thirteen hundred pounds, stolen from Belfield, Billings Co., Dak., May 26. No brand on them when stolen.

A. ANDERSON, Belfield, Dak.
articles.summary: A. Anderson offers $125 for the return of a gray team stolen at Belfield on May 26.

articles.headline: Stockmen's Meeting.
articles.text: There will be a meeting of Bad Lands stockmen at Medora on Tuesday, September 9, 1884, for the purpose of effecting a permanent organization and making the necessary preparations for the fall round-up. A captain for the round-up will also be selected. Let every stockman be present.
articles.summary: Call for a meeting of Bad Lands stockmen at Medora on Sept. 9 to organize permanently and prepare the fall round-up.

articles.text: Last week thirty horses were stolen from John Smith's herd on Alkali creek Montana.
articles.summary: Thirty horses were stolen from John Smith's herd on Alkali creek, Montana.

articles.text: It is estimated that the drive out of the state of Texas for 1884 will foot up 450,000 head of cattle.
articles.summary: The 1884 Texas cattle drive is estimated at 450,000 head.

articles.text: The cattle round-ups in northern Colorado have been ordered stopped until the fever epidemic has passed over.
articles.summary: Northern Colorado round-ups halted for the fever epidemic.

articles.text: For the past six days Colorado beef cattle have been selling in Kansas City at $4.20 to $4.25 for steers whose weight would overgo 1,100 pounds.—[Col. L. S. Record.
articles.summary: Colorado beef steers selling at $4.20–$4.25 in Kansas City.

articles.text: Ninety per cent. of the cattle attacked by the Texas fever have been of the she kind. Many cows have died while their calves have not been affected.—[Col. L. S. Record.
articles.summary: Most Texas fever victims have been cows.

articles.text: The largest ranch in the world is in the Province of Cordoba, Argentine Republic, South America, and is owned by an English syndicate. It comprises 10,400 square miles of land.—[N. M. Stock Grower.
articles.summary: The world's largest ranch is in Cordoba, Argentina.

articles.text: General George B. McClelland is now a cow owner on the western plains. His bovines browse the grass in New Mexico, while Ben Butler and P. T. Barnum have their cows in southern Colorado.—[Col. L. S. Record.
articles.summary: Gen. McClellan, Ben Butler and P. T. Barnum own cattle in the West.

articles.text: The great cattle wealth of the Messrs. Swans, of Wyoming, has been accumulated in the past ten years. They to-day control more cattle than any other syndicate in America, if not in the world.—[Col. L. S. Record.
articles.summary: The Swan brothers of Wyoming control the largest cattle syndicate in America.

articles.text: A cow in County Carlow, Ireland, has produced four heifer calves in ten months. The cow was calved April 4, 1881, had her two first calves on July 25, last year, and two more on the 25th of May, this year.—[N. M. Stock Grower.
articles.summary: An Irish cow produced four heifer calves in ten months.

articles.text: Twenty horses disappeared on Friday night from Mr. Field's herd, which was grazing near town. They are supposed to have been stolen. They are branded M P combined, or half circle R A.—[Livingstone Enterprise.
articles.summary: Twenty horses disappeared from Mr. Field's herd near Livingston, Montana.

articles.text: An exchange says that cattle are perishing in Chihuahua, Mexico, by the drouth. Two thousand died at the hacienda of Agustin Cordero. The dead animals are burned to prevent disease emanating from the frightful mortality.
articles.summary: Drought kills cattle in Chihuahua, Mexico.

articles.text: American cattle are steady at Liverpool at 14 to 15 cents per pound, which is a very good price considering the price on this side of the water. Sheep are going over there at 15 to 16 cents. These prices are for dead weight.—[Col. L. S. Record.
articles.summary: American cattle steady at Liverpool at 14–15 cents.

articles.text: Three hundred young Texas cattle were tramped to death on the Bloomfield range in the Arkansas country during a hail storm one day last week. They stampeded and collided against a wire fence, when the stronger ones killed the weaker ones.—[Col. L. S. Record.
articles.summary: Three hundred Texas cattle trampled to death in a hail-storm stampede.

articles.text: Latest reports from the British markets are a little more encouraging to exporters, best American cattle being quoted at 15 cents per pound, estimated dead weight. The sheep trade was quiet and steady at 15@16 cents for good to choice heavy Americans.
articles.summary: British market quotations for American cattle and sheep.

articles.text: Nearly 700 head of the Continental Land and Cattle Company's cattle were on sale Monday. This company have already sent 4,000 cattle to the Chicago market this season, and they have from 8,000 to 10,000 yet to ship. They have extensive ranches in Texas, Montana and Dakota.—[Breeder's Gazette.
articles.summary: Continental Land and Cattle Company cattle sales at Chicago.

articles.text: A report from the department of agriculture gives the number of live stock in the United States as follows: Horses, 11,169,682; mules, 1,914,126; milch cows, 13,501,206; oxen and other cattle, 29,045,101; sheep, 50,626,626; hogs, 44,200,893, with a total value of $2,467,868,924.
articles.summary: Department of Agriculture livestock census figures.

articles.text: The finest cattle shipped from the ranges thus far this season reached the stock yards Monday last. They were from the pastures of Montana. There were two bunches, 108 head averaging 1,226 pounds, and 290 head averaging 1,211 pounds, and they sold at $5.75 and $6, respectively.—[Breeder's Gazette.
articles.summary: Montana range cattle top the market this season.

articles.text: In the first six months of 1884 a total of 81,016 live cattle were exported from the United States to England, against [illegible] in the same part of 1883. The totals received from all sources in the English markets were respectively 154,060 and 152,369. Of fresh meats the United States furnished 416,638 cwt. in the first six months of 1884, against 376,755 in the same part of 1883.
articles.summary: Live cattle and fresh meat exports to England, first half of 1884.

articles.text: A report came here last Friday, August 2d, that the Kiowa and Comanche Indians were burning the range in the southern part of their reservation, and would keep up the work until the cattle were forced to leave. These Indians have no idea whatever as to the size of their grass bonanza, and although they have been offered much more than the business can stand as a steady drain they persistently want "more." It is said they will drive all the cattle south of the river.—[Mobeetie (Tex.) Panhandle.
articles.summary: Kiowa and Comanche reported burning range to drive off cattle (Texas Panhandle clipping).

articles.text: Never in the history of the cattle business in the west has the outlook been brighter at this season of the year than it now is. With scarcely an exception, the feed on the range is abundant, and the gradual curing of the grass has made it all that could be desired for winter use. Pilgrim cattle have generally reached their new range and will have time to take on flesh and prepare for the winter storms. There is nothing in the air to indicate any material decline in values and cattle owners are generally in a hopeful mood.—[N. W. L. S. Journal.
articles.summary: Range outlook in the West is reported bright.

articles.text: Guard against prairie fires. The season is now approaching when the greatest care should be exercised to prevent the destruction of grass. Grass is money, and a widespread prairie fire will mean heavy loss to cattle owners next spring. Impress upon your employes the necessity of being careful with camp fires. A strong breeze will scatter sparks to spread desolation over the plains. The railroads have, we believe, complied with the statute compelling the plowing of fire guards on each side of the track, which will reduce the risk of fire from one source. Now it remains for ranchmen themselves to look after the rest, and see that tons of valuable grass are not wasted by the flames.—[N. M. Stock Grower.
articles.summary: Warning to ranchmen to guard against prairie fires.

articles.text: Several of the principal stockmen of the country south and southeast of San Antonio who came up last week wore sorrowful faces. They say the country has dried up more rapidly within the past month than they ever knew it to do in twice the time, and the grass is parched, and there are many places where hundreds of acres are almost barren. Those who have obligated themselves to pay money, find refusals to let them have it on every hand, and unless men determine to be lenient and carry one another there must come heavy reverses, and ruin in some instances. The sale of stock is very slow, and there is nothing like the demand of last spring at a discount even of twenty per cent. on the spring prices. We hope for better times, but that is all we can do.—[Texas Wool-Grower.
articles.summary: Drought and tight money distress South Texas stockmen.

articles.headline: Marketing Cattle.
articles.text:
It is one thing to raise cattle for market and another to know when and how to get them there. When to ship and when to hold require as much judgment and, it may be added, experience as it does to make purchases and care for the cattle after they are bought.

Any one who has closely observed the course of events at any one of the leading markets of the country for a number of years cannot but have arrived at the above conclusion.

The raising of cattle, as a general thing, is a profitable thing when well managed, but like every other pursuit in life it requires experience and judgment. A few dollars a head lost on the number of cattle owned are not often missed, for there is a profit anyhow, but if those few dollars had been added to the sum total they would undoubtedly be appreciated.

It has been observed that some cattle raisers, year after year, manage so as to reach the markets at a time and with their cattle in such condition as to realize prices which, when compared with those realized by their neighbors, make a good profit on the larger amount obtained, to say nothing of the satisfactory manner in which their business appears to be managed.

There are parties engaged in feeding cattle, who exercise poor judgment in their purchases, the handling of the cattle after making the purchase and then again in selling them for beef, whereas there are others who move along quietly, manage their affairs smoothly and who invariably come out ahead.

There are thousands of dollars lost annually by cattle raisers, who do not pay sufficient attention to the details of the business, and who, instead of watching the markets and the course of events, move along as if every season was alike and values were the same from year to year.—[Kansas City L. S. Indicator.
articles.summary: Clipped essay on the judgment needed in marketing cattle.

articles.text: Frank Turner returned from St. Paul last evening.
articles.summary: Frank Turner returned from St. Paul.

articles.text: [Alex.?] Metzger, of Bismarck, was in town Tuesday.
articles.summary: Metzger of Bismarck visited Medora Tuesday.

articles.text: Edward G. Bailey, of Billings, M. T., was in town last Monday.
articles.summary: Edward G. Bailey of Billings, M. T., visited Monday.

articles.text: Marquis de Mores left for the east last Sunday on his special car Livingston.
articles.summary: The Marquis de Mores left for the east Sunday in his special car Livingston.

articles.text: Bob Roberts went to Bismarck last Tuesday. He will be gone several days.
articles.summary: Bob Roberts went to Bismarck Tuesday.

articles.text: F. B. Allen, secretary of the N. P. Ref. Car Co., was in town the fore part of the week.
articles.summary: F. B. Allen, secretary of the N. P. Refrigerator Car Co., was in town early in the week.

articles.text: D. K. Wade, of the Lemoyne Cattle Company, came in from his ranch on Tuesday.
articles.summary: D. K. Wade of the Lemoyne Cattle Company came in from his ranch Tuesday.

articles.text: The platform scales, trucks, letter press, etc., for the forwarders' office arrived yesterday.
articles.summary: Equipment for the forwarders' office arrived.

articles.text: Baron von Hoffmann went down to Dickinson Tuesday to witness the shipping of some cattle.
articles.summary: Baron von Hoffmann went to Dickinson to see cattle shipped.

articles.text: M. Wadsworth, of the Bad Lands Cattle Company, came up from his ranch on last Saturday.
articles.summary: M. Wadsworth of the Bad Lands Cattle Company came up from his ranch Saturday.

articles.text: The past two days have been among the hottest of the season, the thermometer registering 95 degrees in the shade.
articles.summary: Heat reached 95 degrees in the shade.

articles.text: Peter Book has a force of men at work putting a new foundation under the cold storage building. It will be substantial this time.
articles.summary: Peter Book's crew is putting a new foundation under the cold storage building.

articles.text: Marquis de Mores received three fine elk horns the other day. They are fine ones, and for size they exceed anything we ever saw.
articles.summary: The Marquis de Mores received three large elk horns.

articles.text: T. J. Kerr, the genial traveling auditor of the Northern Pacific Refrigerator Car Company, left for Helena on last Friday evening.
articles.summary: T. J. Kerr left for Helena Friday evening.

articles.text: J. D. Garver, formerly of Bismarck, arrived here yesterday with his family and a stock of goods. He will open a hardware store and tin shop.
articles.summary: J. D. Garver arrived to open a hardware store and tin shop.

articles.text: J. H. Simpson, of Hughes & Simpson, was a guest of the Marquis for a few days. He left here Monday morning for Dickinson to ship some cattle.
articles.summary: J. H. Simpson, guest of the Marquis, left Monday for Dickinson to ship cattle.

articles.text: C. H. Skelton, representing Strong, Hackett & Co., of St. Paul, has been here a day or two replenishing the hardware stocks of our merchants.
articles.summary: Hardware salesman C. H. Skelton of St. Paul visited.

articles.text: Lovers of fruit and incidently a little fun will be grieved to learn that the wild plums, of which there promised to be an abundance, were all knocked off by the hail.
articles.summary: Hail knocked off the wild plum crop.

articles.text: The company's lumber yard has been enclosed by a high board fence. Probably to protect the lumber from being blown away by the gentle zephyrs, such as we had last week.
articles.summary: The company's lumber yard has been fenced.

articles.text: The two horsethieves, Henry Scott and Clay Layton, who were arrested near Miles City for stealing four horses from Archie Morton of South Heart, passed through on No. 2 this morning in charge of Sheriff Cuskelly, of Dickinson.
articles.summary: Horse thieves Scott and Layton passed through on No. 2 in custody of Sheriff Cuskelly.

articles.text: Among the curiosities of the museum in the Cow Boy office is a horned toad, which has been kept in a cigar box several weeks without any visible means of support. Yesterday the discovery was made that it had seven young ones.
articles.summary: The horned toad kept at the Cow Boy office produced seven young.

articles.text: Dr. F. Harck, of Germany, who has been visiting here as the guest of Marquis de Mores, left for the Yellowstone Park Sunday evening. From there he goes to San Francisco via Portland, from which point he sails for Japan and China.
articles.summary: Dr. F. Harck of Germany, guest of the Marquis, left for Yellowstone Park.

articles.text: During the recent storm that portion of the roof of the depot covering the telegraph and ticket office was badly demolished. The ceiling is good enough to keep out the dew, but our station agent, Mr. Brinker, not being webfooted finds it quite unpleasant when it rains.
articles.summary: The recent storm damaged the depot roof.

articles.text: O. F. Lindquist, an artist in the line of stone, enameled brick and terra-cotta, is here and will test some of our clay, which, from a test of a small sample sent him last season, he is satisfied is of excellent quality. If the requsite inducement is held out he will locate a manufactory of his wares here.
articles.summary: O. F. Lindquist is testing local clay with a view to starting a brick and terra-cotta works.

articles.text: In another column we publish a call for a meeting of Bad Lands stockmen. The object of this meeting is for the purpose of establishing a permanent organization of Bad Lands stockmen. The necessity of such an organization is very apparent, and is a movement in which every stockman should personally interest himself.
articles.summary: Editorial urging stockmen to attend the organizing meeting.

articles.text: Last evening Henry, who drives the team of gray horses belonging to A. T. Packard, drove to the store and went in after a sack of oats. The horses becoming frightened at the train started for home at a lively gait, but brought up on the river bank astride a stump, causing a dislocated reach, broken single-tree and harness somewhat demoralized.
articles.summary: Packard's gray team ran away when frightened by a train.

articles.text: The surveyors who are making the official plat of this and adjacent townships were here Tuesday, enabling us to locate ourselves, so to speak. The town of Medora is in the northeast one-quarter of section 27 and northwest one-quarter of section 26, township 140, north of range 102, west. The section line runs a little to the west of the freight house, between Medora hall and the hotel, on and nearly parallel to Third street, thus cutting the town nearly in the middle. The section corner is at the foot of the bluff north of town.
articles.summary: Government surveyors platting the township located Medora in sections 26 and 27, T140N, R102W.

articles.text: The storm of a week ago Monday seems to have been widespread, at lesat the rain, as nearly all our Dakota exchanges have accounts of a heavy rain-fall. At Deadwood the signal office records show a fall of 1¼ inches in about 36 hours, which is a very heavy fall of water for any country. In this locality its freaks were peculiar. Coming from the west, where it did most damage, it broke all the glass on the south side of buildings at Medora, while at Belfield the glass was broken on the west side, and the storm was accompanied by terrific thunder and lightning. Fields of grain and gardens were entirely destroyed, cherry and plum bushes stripped of their fruit and rabbits killed.
articles.summary: The storm of Monday, Aug. 18 broke window glass at Medora and Belfield and destroyed crops and gardens.

articles.text: Preparations for the stage line are fast nearing completion, and another week of good weather will see the stations completed and hay put up on this end of the line. A. T. Packard, general manager, and J. C. Fisher, local manager, who started for the Hills on Friday last, have no doubt ere this effected arrangements at that end. Four eleven-passenger Concord coaches and the harness arrived here on Tuesday, and Mr. Barr writes from Helena that the horses would be shipped on the 27th, yesterday, so that by Saturday at the farthest the horses and the balance of the coaches will be here. Supt. Deffebach will at once distribute the stock, and by the first of the following week we may reasonably expect to see the coaches running.
articles.summary: Stage line preparations: Packard and Fisher went to the Hills, four Concord coaches arrived, and horses were shipped from Helena; coaches expected to run early in September.

articles.headline: NOTICE OF CONTEST.
articles.text:
U. S. Land Office, Bismarck, Dak., July 9, 1884.

Complaint having been entered at this office by John Weber against John Peehn for abandoning his homestead entry No. 1533, dated April 9, 1883, upon the SE¼, section 20, township 140, range 99, in Billings county, Dakota, with a view to the cancellation of said entry; the said parties are hereby summoned to appear at this office on the 21st day of August, 1884, at 10 o'clock A. M., to respond and furnish testimony concerning said alleged abandonment.

J. A. Rea, Register.
O. F. Davis, Att'y. for Contestant. 24-5t
articles.summary: Land office notice of John Weber's contest of John Peehn's homestead entry in Billings county.
